toolCalls.name: StructuredOutput

output.methodChoice: Read the initial evidence, then collected X3 (Analyzer B event log) and X9 (vendor correspondence) to test the sampling-glitch and lot-shift explanations.
output.brief:
What is probably going on: the 11 November Level 2 potassium flag looks like a single chance or sampling outlier, not a fault in the reagent lot or the analyzer. Across 182 QC runs there was only one violation, the repeat passed, and Analyzer B's potassium results matched Analyzer A's within 0.2 mmol/L on 43 re-tested samples. Staffing did not cause missed QC; every scheduled run completed. The vendor also sees no problem. The Ward 6 high potassiums are better explained by delayed sample transport during the tube outage, and about half were run on Analyzer A, so the analyzer is not the main suspect.

How sure: moderately. We cannot confirm whether the 14:10 result was a short aspiration, because the instrument cannot detect one.

What to sign off: do not recall the patients, do not widen the limits, and do not record the cause as confirmed. Before returning Analyzer B to service, have the supervisor review the 186 flagged results and add extra Level 2 checks each shift for a week. Ask clinical staff to request repeat samples for the 14 high results, and prioritise restoring the Ward 6 tube service or a faster porter route.
